posts.content:
AI made content production close to free. Conversion is the only scarce metric left that matters.

That sounds like good news. It is not.
The pattern shows up in the numbers before the strategy deck.
Token spend climbs.
Content output climbs.
Closed-won stays flat.
We see it often enough that it is now a buying trigger in our own ICP work: AI spend rising while conversion sits still.
When both move together, the system is working. When only one moves, you have bought volume, not qualified conversations.
The instinct is to fix this with better writing. Tighter subject lines, sharper hooks, more personalisation.
That is treating a targeting failure as a craft failure.
Anyone can tailor now. The scarce asset is knowing what to tailor to, and being able to defend that answer to a board.
Most teams cannot. They can state their ICP in a sentence. They cannot tell you which of their last forty closed-won deals actually match it, or which channel produced the ones that did.
Without that, personalisation is guesswork with better grammar.
Two habits fix it, and neither one is a campaign.
No channel gets written off until past performance has actually been examined. Paid is dead, events do not scale, outbound is over. Sometimes the channel was fine and the offer was wrong.

Validate the plan against your live pipeline gap, not against best practice. Best practice is an average. Your gap is a number: this quarter's pipeline against this quarter's target.

Here is the test you can run this week.
Pull your last forty closed-won and closed-lost deals. Score them against your written ICP.
If more than a third of your wins fall outside it, your offer is not mistargeted. Your profile is. Fix that before you generate another asset.
If you want a second set of eyes, we start with a read-only CRM gap analysis. No budget, no contract. You see real findings about your own funnel first.
Details in the comments.

My son's swim practice is Monday at 4:30, and I usually miss it.

For most of this year, I treated that like weather, something happening to me rather than something I was choosing.

The 4:30 slot sits exactly where deals need the most attention, so there was always something that seemed to have a claim on my time.

A few weeks ago I stopped trying to fight for the time back and wrote it into my AI revenue engine I use to run my pipeline.

There's a rule in it now that runs on Monday before the day starts, and when nothing is booked after 3:30, it tells me to leave at 4:15.

It says so in the morning, unprompted, while the day can still be changed.

Then I went back and looked at the Mondays I'd already lost. It was really eye-opening.

Now and going forward, my weeks are structured with me as the operator.

Nothing had taken the slot, and nobody had outbid my son.

I just wasn't looking at four o'clock on a Monday, which is the only moment that information was worth anything.

Founders, you already know which thing this is for you, because you probably say it out loud to your spouse or just in your head all the time, and haven't taken control of it.

Your not a victim to the constant stress your pipeline or other sheep herding tasks. You might feel like your dropping the ball because nothing in your week is deployed to defend your time.

I aim to leverage our current tools to stay productive and still deliver the highest-quality work.

He isn't going to be this age for very long, and the tools and resources God has allowed us to have can let us take control of it.

posts.content:
Yesterday I gave my AI revenue sculpting system one instruction.

Read the last 120 days of my email, Slack, and CRM before answering any prompt, so every answer I get is answered in context, making my output 10X better.

It sounded obviously right when I said it, and more context does usually mean better answers.

Then I looked at how much data the instruction would actually have to read every time, and the literal version was impossible to build.

My CRM holds 36,436 deal records as of this morning. Slack hands the system back twenty search results at a time. The email window alone held 201 threads when it got measured yesterday.

Evaluating all of that before answering one question I was prompting it for would take minutes per prompt, and the answer would come back as AI slop, buried under context that has nothing to do with the question.

That was honestly a little humbling, because the instruction was mine, and the data against it came out of the connectors I told the system to check every time I prompt.

So now the system runs it in two layers instead.

A small ledger, about 14 kilobytes, rebuilt on a routine every morning at 6:12 am, carries every open deal, every counterparty, and every open loop I haven't checked yet, and it is only trusted to say where to look.

Before the system states anything as a fact, it opens the live record: the deal, the thread, the calendar invite.

The reason for the split is that a summary written yesterday is a memory, and between yesterday's count and this morning's, the same CRM added twelve deal records.

If you're a founder wiring AI into your revenue motion, you've probably given it some version of my instruction: "know everything about my company, and always answer me with the full context of my situation."

Stored context earns its place by pointing at the right record, and the live data is what will provide the best answer.

Ask your AI where the number in its last answer came from. If it probably will give a stored summary it never checked against the live record, you now know which of its answers need a second look.

Somewhere between $5M and $50M ARR, your operating review becomes a wall of numbers that move weekly. New MRR. Pipeline created. Activation rate. Logo churn. Net revenue retention.

There is 1 blind spot, and the blind spot is expensive.

The work that moves those numbers most seldom shows up on that screen in the quarter it happens.

The onboarding rebuild shows nothing for ninety days, then quietly lifts retention for every cohort that follows. The pricing and packaging project, the one moving you from flat seats to tiers your customers actually expand inside, is invisible the entire time it is being modeled. The ICP narrowing that has the team declining deals you would have taken last year reads on the dashboard as a soft month, not as a strategy. Your new revenue leader's first thirty days produce all map and no territory. And some quarters there really is a big enterprise proposal sitting silent in a procurement review, moving and immovable at the same time... lol

Here’s the discipline that keeps great strategy from getting killed too early: Before the work starts, define 3 things:- the result it should produce, the metric it should move, the date you’ll evaluate it (That might look like: an onboarding rebuild tied to a day-90 cohort readout) - a pricing project tied to a CFO-approved model and migration plan, a repositioning effort tied to your sales team pitching the new narrative by a specific date

Then give that work a permanent place in your operating review before the metrics move. If the work can name its output, it’s probably a moving strategy. If it can’t, it may just be drift. 

What’s the highest-value invisible work in your business this quarter?

posts.content:
Every SaaS contract contains two purchases.

The first one is on the order form. Seats, licenses, tiers, the feature list that your sales team demoed. The second one lives in your customer's head: the outcome they believe those licenses are going to buy them.

Renewal is decided by the second purchase. Your order form only describes the first.

When the two drift apart, it does not look like churn at first. It looks like a customer who rips things apart. They count logins. They question a price increase line. They want the feature roadmap before they will book the QBR. Auditing the software is what buying-the-artifact looks like six months in. Customers who bought into the outcome the platform promised behave differently. 

They bring you their next problem instead of your feature list.

Somewhere between $5M and $50M ARR, this gap stops being a customer-success anecdote and becomes your NRR line. A book of customers who bought features expands at the pace of seat count. A book of customers who bought outcomes expands at the pace of their ambition, and it defends the price increase your CFO wants next year.

The uncomfortable part is where the gap gets created. It's not created at the renewal. It is created in the first proposal, and how your money model integrates to the onboarding flow, and the QBR template. If those motions talk seats and features, you have trained the customer to measure seats and features. If every one of them names the outcome and the number it moves, you have trained the customer to measure that instead.

The sale really never ends.. hahah

An exercise worth an hour this month: ask five customers what they think they are paying for, and write down their exact words. Then put their answers next to your renewal or upsell pitch. If they name features, your expansion is capped at headcount. 

If they name outcomes, you are holding pricing power you may not be using.

What does your best customer think they bought from you? And does your order form agree?

posts.content:
Most marketing failures are stage mismatches in disguise.

I have spent the last seven months in conversations with B2B SaaS founders running every kind of GTM motion you can imagine. The pattern I keep seeing is the same. The founder is trying to do the next stage's job before they have finished the current one. There are four stages. Each one asks a completely different question.

Stage 1. MVP. The question is, can you build it? Marketing's job here is one thing. Stop your team from spending money on demand gen they will throw away in nine months. No paid ads. No SDR team. Just enough content to validate that the pain point is real and the language you use to describe it lands.

Stage 2. PMF. The question is: will they pay? Marketing's job is narrower than founders think. Find the smallest possible ICP that converts at 25 percent or better. Most founders try to expand here. The right move is to narrow. The trap is adding features when the real fix is narrower positioning.

Stage 3. T2D3. The question is, can you scale it? Triple, triple, double, double, double your revenue. The math takes you from one million ARR to one hundred. Marketing's job is now a system, not a campaign. ICP, watering hole, demand gen, ABM, content. All channels feeding the same pipeline. The trap most companies fall into here is keeping the CEO in the CMO seat. The reason most B2B SaaS companies die between three and twenty million ARR is the founder cannot let go of being the marketer.

Stage 4. Profitability. The question is, can you keep it? Positive EBITDA at your own pace. You stop selling to the next round and start selling to your customers.

This is the only stage where freedom of choice becomes a real asset on the balance sheet. The hard truth. The campaign that works at Stage 2 will fail at Stage 3. The agency that built your Stage 3 motion is the wrong agency for Stage 4.

The CMO that gets you from PMF to T2D3 is probably not the CMO that gets you to profitability. Stage mismatches are quiet. They look like marketing failures. They are usually maturity failures.

Where is your B2B SaaS company actually living right now? Be honest. Pick one.

Last week I sent 15 outbound emails before my coffee got cold.
Everyone led with the same line. 'The real bottleneck is positioning, not leads. Wrong audience, wrong message, wrong timing.'

The execs who wrote back had one thing in common. They could describe their buyer at Rung 4. The ones who never replied were stuck at Rung 1 or Rung 2 and did not know it.

Framework Mondays, Post 2. The ICP Narrowing Ladder. Four rungs. Only one of them is a wedge that dials in your true winning target ICP.

Rung 1. Everyone. The category is not an ICP. "We help B2B SaaS companies" is a delete key waiting to happen.

Rung 2. A vertical. 'B2B SaaS in fintech.' Better. Still too broad to price against, still too broad to know which channels have trust, still too broad to write one message that lands.

Rung 3. A stage and a vertical. 'Series A B2B SaaS in fintech.' Now you can price. Now you can hire. Now you can name three watering holes without stalling. This is the rung most founders stop at, and it is the rung most agencies bill against.

Rung 4. A stage and a vertical and a pain. 'Series A B2B SaaS in fintech losing pilots at the RFP stage.' This is a wedge. Every word does work. Every founder in this ICP knows exactly who they are within three seconds of reading the sentence.

The exercise for this week. Write your ICP on one line. Read it back. Which rung are you on?

If you are honest and it is Rung 1 or Rung 2, your problem is not marketing.

article.title: The ICP Narrowing Ladder: The Four Rungs Between You and Buyers Who Reply
article.subtitle: Braison Murgai
article.linkLabel: Open article: The ICP Narrowing Ladder: The Four Rungs Between You and Buyers Who Reply by Braison Murgai • 7 min read
article.description: Ask a B2B SaaS founder who their ideal customer is and listen for the first two words. More often than not, they're "anyone who."I posted a four-rung

posts.content:
"We buy a tool before we hire a person."
That is the rule at a company doing about seven million in revenue, where the entire marketing function is one person.

And the rule works, which is what makes it hard to argue with.
I hear a version of it most weeks now. It has overtaken price as the hardest objection in my pipeline.

Four companies I met with this month had already run that test.

One reduced engineering teams from about 160 to about 60 by utilizing AI agents. That is real compression, and I have no reason to doubt it. 

Then, in the same conversation, he told me his marketing team was struggling to keep up with everything engineering was now shipping and asked whether we sell marketing agents too.

One built an AI outbound workflow agent, read its output, called it spamming, and then switched it off. What replaced it was press coverage and a small dinner series, neither of which scales and both of which take real human effort, and both of which are now outperforming the automated version they turned off.

One ran the productivity claim against his own benchmark data instead of taking it on faith. 

He found that nobody is getting more than 10 to 15 percent, even the teams being most diligent about it, against a promise of ten times.

And our own team sent 2,758 cold emails this year on exactly that logic, which was that the tooling would carry the volume for us. 

Two people replied.

Engineering compressed because somebody had already decided what to build. 

The agents had something to execute against.

Marketing is the function where nothing gets defined until a human decides who it's for.

That decision has never been the expensive part to execute. 

It has been the expensive part to make.

A tool will execute a decision very cheaply. It will not decide for you.

If your marketing team is one person and your growth has stagnated, you have been buying capacity. The thing you are short of is the decisive action.

'Everything in SaaS is compressing right now with AI.'

It came out of my mouth mid-sentence on a client call Monday, and I have been chewing on it since.

In 2020, a founder pitching Series A modeled 12 to 18 months to prove ROI. The buyer would evaluate for a quarter. Implementation took another quarter. First measurable value in month six. Full ROI clarity in month twelve. The math worked because the buyer would still be around at month twelve.

In 2026, the model has to bend or break. Buyers evaluate in three weeks. Implementation is two clicks. Value is expected in month one, ROI clarity in month three, the expansion conversation in month six. The window shrank by two-thirds.

Start with your investor deck. If it models an 18-month payback, you are pitching a 2022 company in a 2026 room. Rebuild the model before the next partner meeting does it for you.

Then look at onboarding. Your sales team is not slow. Your onboarding is. Every extra week between contract signature and first measurable value is a week the buyer's board is asking why they signed.

Then look at your reporting cadence. Quarterly reviews for a 12-month contract are over. Weekly ROI check-ins are the new floor. If you cannot report ROI in week two, the contract already feels stale by month three.
There is a good version of this and a bad version. The bad version is short-termism dressed up as urgency. Founders ripping up plans every three weeks, chasing the next dopamine hit of adoption.

The good version is discipline on a faster clock. Same math. Same ICP. Same retention target, reported weekly instead of quarterly. The founders who win the compression kept the discipline and changed the calendar.

Last week my team went from discovery-call transcripts to a full first-draft proposal in one afternoon.

Drafting that document used to take the better part of a week. The compression is real, and it is also the least interesting part of the story. The interesting part is the rule that makes the speed safe.
AI-Forward GTM Lab. The framework is called Hours and Promises.
Every document in your sales process is two things at once. Hours: the drafting, the recap, the research, the formatting, the tailoring. Promises: the scope, the price, the dates, the outcomes your company is now on the hook for.

Hand AI every hour you can find—transcript to recap in minutes. Discovery notes to first draft in an afternoon. Account research to a briefing before the second call. This is where the machine is legitimately excellent, and where most B2B SaaS sales teams are still burning their best sellers' calendars.

Never hand AI a promise you made in the meeting. Scope, price, timeline, and outcomes get read and owned by a human before anything ships. And not just any human. The person who has to deliver the work reads every promise in the document because sellers read proposals optimistically and the people delivering the service read them through their calendar.

The hours you reclaim are only worth something if your licensee or buyer receives them. The follow-up that lands the same afternoon while the conversation is still warm. The time & money savings and workflow automation built on their numbers instead of a template. 

The proposal that arrives in days, tailored, instead of in three weeks, generic. Buyers will feel the tempo.

article.description: I was reading 44 call transcripts for a completely different reason when I noticed it.Four of those founders had told me, unprompted, that they found

posts.content:
Between 2015 and 2022, distribution was the moat. The companies that won B2B SaaS in that window won because they built distribution before their competitors did. HubSpot built inbound. Mailchimp built brand. Drift built conversational. Gong built sales intelligence. Owning a channel meant winning a category.

Between 2024 and now, distribution became the commodity.

Every B2B SaaS team has access to the same playbook, the same tools, and the same content engine. Cold outbound is a commodity. SEO is a commodity. LinkedIn ghostwriting is a commodity. Webinars are a commodity. Even your podcast is a commodity. The infrastructure that took five years and ten million dollars to build in 2018 takes a Saturday and a hundred dollars in API credits now.

The implication for B2B SaaS leadership is uncomfortable. The thing you spent the last four years building is no longer a moat. The investment was correct in 2020. It is depreciating in 2026.

The new moat is on the other side of the workflow. Creativity. Taste. Point of view. The ability to say something true that nobody else in your category is willing to say.

Three things every B2B SaaS leader should internalize before Q4.

First. Distribution is no longer scarce. Stop investing in it as if it is. 
Move budget from channel-acquisition to creativity-acquisition.  Second. SEO and cold outbound are commodities. Treat them like utilities. Have them, do not over-invest in them. The marginal hour you spend on cold subject lines is no longer the marginal hour with the highest return. High-quality outbound work clearly outperforms mass distribution.  

Third. The companies winning in 2026 are not louder. They are sharper. They have an actual point of view. 

They are willing to be wrong in public. They publish their frameworks, their losses, their philosophy. Their audience trusts them because the content earns the trust.

posts.content:
A SaaS founder once lost a $60k enterprise deal because the case study his team sent was one tier too left-field for the buyer.

The buyer read it, said "great numbers, not us," and the deal died in procurement.

That is the pattern I see every week across the pipelines I review. Not a product problem. A proof problem.

Welcome back to Framework Mondays. 

The Proof Stack.

Four levels of proof your team ships to a buyer, ranked by how much trust each earns from a mid-market or enterprise operator.

Level 1. The category benchmark. "The average B2B SaaS company grows MQLs by 20 percent." Gartner and G2. Every competitor in your category cites the same numbers. Your buyer has already read them.

Level 2. Your logo wall. A named case study. One metric. One quarter. Where most GTM teams stop. Where most enterprise buyers mentally deduct 40 percent for the compression tax.

Level 3. A peer said it. A named customer at your prospect's size, in your prospect's vertical, using your prospect's own vocabulary. Trust compounds here. The metric matters less than the language.

Level 4. Live, in their tool. A number pulled from your prospect's own data, running inside your product. A dashboard they can validate against their reality in ten seconds. Rare. Expensive to build. Nearly unbeatable in a bake-off.

Monday rule for your GTM team. On every stalled deal, check which level your team last shipped. If it's Level 1 or 2, that is a discovery gap, not a proof gap. The next move is not a better case study. It is a better first call, one that earns access to build Level 4.

A deal I closed as lost eleven days ago came back this week.

Same buyers. Same product. Same use case. New row at the top of the pipeline, budget attached, asking me to prepare the proposal by EOW.

I want to say I saw it coming. I did not.

Something I have started tracking, quietly, is how often my closed-lost deals resurface inside ninety days. Right now the number is running higher than I would have guessed. Closer to one in six than the five percent Winning by Design put in the study I read a year ago.

Which changes how I write the close-lost email.

The old close-lost email is a wave and a smile. "Best of luck, glad to reconnect if things change." Polite. Brief. Zero signal.

But, my new approach is more probing.. What decided it. Who else weighed in. What number would have moved you. Three sentences, one honest ask but subtly, and it really does lean on your relationship with the prospect too. I really like to be as polite, genuine and understanding as possible.

I'll usually Send it two days after the loss, before the memory blurs.

The buyer that ghosted you at 30 percent is often still in the same position with the same problem three months later. 

The only question is whether they call you when the problem comes back. Polite obscures that. A pointed email keeps the door open on the right terms.

If you have a closed-lost list from Q1, it is not a graveyard. It is a warm cohort you may not have communicated with correctly.

"Capture as it happens."

That was the instruction my AI operating system wrote for itself yesterday, in its own rules file, about logging the ideas that come out of our working sessions.

Today I asked it to start keeping that log.

It went looking first, and found the instruction already sitting there, twenty-four hours old.

It had never fired once.

Every entry in the log came from a session where I asked for it out loud, in the moment.
Meanwhile, 49 session transcripts and roughly 68 megabytes of my own prompting had piled up on my disk in three days, and nothing had ever read a line of them.

The instruction lived in a file that only loads when something opens it, and nothing opens that file while you are in the middle of the work.

Anyone calling themselves a GTM engineer right now is writing instructions to a system like this one.

An instruction is not a mechanism.

A prompt library, a rules file, the block of instructions at the top of your context window: every one of those is a wish until something opens it at the moment the work is happening.

So go and open the rules you've written for your AI.

For each one, can you name what loads it?

posts.content:
The cheapest revenue you'll ever lock in is hiding in a box most founders never look in.

In a revenue planning session this week, I caught myself sketching the Ansoff Matrix on screen — the 60-year-old growth grid everyone nods at, and nobody actually uses. 

There are only four ways to grow:

→ Sell more of what you have to the market you have (penetration) → Take what you have to a new market (market development) → Build something new for the customers you already have (product development) → Build something new for a market you don't have yet (diversification = the hail mary pass)

Here's the trap. Almost every founder dumps the marketing budget into box one: new logos, more pipeline, top-of-funnel. It's the most expensive box on the grid — you pay full CAC for a stranger every single time.

Meanwhile, box three sits untouched. A new product for customers who already trust you, have already cleared procurement, and have already renewed. That's the lowest-revenue stream in the entire business, and most teams treat it as an afterthought.

Expansion revenue doesn't pay CAC twice. Crediting Stijn Hendrikse for this one.. "Your current customers are your biggest moat"

Before you greenlight another acquisition campaign, put your actual roadmap on the grid. If everything you're spending sits in one box, you don't have a growth strategy — you have a habit.

Which box is funding your next quarter?

posts.content:
Eleven years before I wrote the words ACV, CAC, or NRR in a Slack channel, I was running the same three equations under different names. I was selling credit card processing. Door to door. The vocabulary nobody at the B2B SaaS conferences used. The math every B2B SaaS team is now obsessed with.

Translation 1. Average Ticket became ACV. In payments, your average ticket was per-swipe revenue across the book. The math was identical to annual contract value in SaaS. A restaurant doing 90K in monthly volume at 0.5 percent margin paid me the same way an enterprise customer at 90K ACV pays a B2B SaaS rep. The shirt changed. The math did not.

Translation 2. Payback Period became CAC Payback. In payments, payback was how many months of processing it took to recoup the cost of standing up the account. Setup fees, free terminals, the dinner you bought when you closed. In SaaS, we call it CAC payback. Same math. Same anxiety when it slipped past twelve months.

Translation 3. Annual Retention became NRR. In payments, annual retention was the percentage of merchants still on file at month 13. In SaaS, we call it net revenue retention. The expansion math layered on top is new. The base discipline of asking who is still here a year later is the same exercise I ran on my book every January.

Here is the lesson I wish I had learned earlier. The vocabulary changed when I got to Kalungi. The economics. And if you cannot run unit economics and show the ROI value on a napkin in the parking lot, the board deck will not save you.

If you came up through restaurants, real estate, or merchant services, you learned it standing in front of someone who could say no to your face. Both paths get you to the same place.

posts.content:
“Which channels should we be on?”

I heard this twice last week, from two different B2B SaaS companies, in two different verticals, at two very different price points.

Both times I noticed, the honest answer was the same—wrong question. The right question is: does your buyer actually trust the medium of communication?

Framework Mondays: The Trust Geography Map.
Picture your market as three rings.

The center is the Watering Hole. The two or three places your ICP already gathers and already has guards down in terms of environment. A niche community, one conference that matters, a Slack group, a newsletter they actually read. Smallest reach on the map. Highest trust transfer per dollar.
The middle ring is Borrowed Trust. Places your buyer hears about you through someone they already trust. Peer referrals. Partner intros. Your own closed-lost list, which knows you better than any cold audience ever will.

The outer ring is the Noise Field. Cold email, cold ads, cold everything. Every competitor you have is out there shouting at the same people. Trust starts at zero, and you pay for every inch of it.

Most budgets for SaaS companies are built from the outside in. Fill the ad channels first, then hope word of mouth shows up on its own. The math runs the other way. A dollar spent in the center ring converts at a multiple of the same dollar spent in the outer ring, and the center ring is usually cheaper.

A simple rule for your team. List every channel you spent attention on last quarter and place each one on the map. If more than half the spend sits in the Noise Field while your Watering Hole goes unfunded, you have found your CAC problem before your board does.

Where does your best-converting channel sit on this map? And is that where your budget sits?

posts.content:
PLG is a magnet. ABM is a spear.

Most B2B SaaS companies only have the magnet.

The magnet pulls people in — signups, free trials, inbound demos. And for $0–$5M ARR, it’s beautiful. Efficient. Scalable.

But magnets don’t work on enterprise or large corporate accounts.

The VP of Operations with a $55K budget isn’t going to sign up for a free trial. The CTO at a Fortune 500 isn’t Googling your product category and clicking “Start Free.”

Enterprise buyers need to be found, targeted, and engaged across multiple channels simultaneously. That’s the spear.

ABM means your list building, your content, your SDR sequences, your LinkedIn outreach, and your paid targeting are all hitting the same accounts at the same time.

You don’t kill the magnet. You layer the spear on top.

The magnet feeds brand awareness. The spear hunts the accounts that will never self-serve into the funnel.

#ABM #AccountBasedMarketing #B2BSaaS #PLG #SalesLedGrowth #GTM

100 million blog posts per day.

That’s where we are in 2026.
Not because more humans are writing so much (obviously).
AI removed the friction from production entirely.

Every B2B SaaS company from seed to Series D now has the same superpower.
Infinite, cheap content.

And most people are not increasing revenue with it.

Because the attention economy is zero-sum.
More content doesn’t grow the pool of buyer attention.
It dilutes it.

The signal-to-noise ratio has collapsed.
Buyers have tuned out by default.

The companies that understand this are pulling back on volume
and investing in precise marketing tactics.

The ones that don’t are going to spend 2026
wondering why their output doubled
while their pipeline flatlined.

A founder of a B2B SaaS company pinged me eight weeks ago about getting his news-to-AI startup ready for go-to-market. He had built something genuinely rare, a search and retrieval as a service API for news publishers feeding the AI ecosystem. Intelligence agencies, media monitoring platforms, and AI workflows that need trustworthy sourcing. What he didn't have was a GTM motion. Friday, we signed. The fractional CMO is locked in. Kickoff is on the calendar. Three things made this one simple with a clear path to strong growth:

1. The ICP was obvious. When publishers want to monetize through AI, AI platforms need trusted retrieval. 

2. The ACV math held up. We modeled a clear revenue map in year one without inflating assumptions. 

3. The founder said yes to a real fractional CMO with demand gen experience, not a back-end coordinator with the title. Most pre-PMF B2B SaaS deals stall on the third one. If you're a founder still doing the marketing yourself at $1M-$5M ARR, the question isn't whether you need a T2D3 AI-enabled CMO. It's whether you'll hire one before your competitor does.

posts.content:
Stijn dropped a link in our Slack Sunday morning.

A full website. Text, structure, navigation, images. Auto-generated by the T2D3 OS he has been building. Input was one ICP definition, one persona list, and a couple of example URLs he pointed at as brand reference.

I opened it and clicked around for twenty minutes before I could say what had actually changed. Then I got there.

Marketing agencies have priced themselves around a three-week site build. Discovery. Wireframes. Design. Copy. Build. Launch. The clock ran because every step needed a human to look at it.

That clock ran out now, at least for the first pass.

What is left is the work AI is bad at. Deciding what your company actually stands for. Picking the one message the site defends. Sitting in enough discovery calls to know which sentence the buyer says right before they lean in. Also, understanding why your current customers actually purchased from you.

The good version of AI-forward marketing looks like this. AI takes the mechanical hours. The human takes the two or three decisions that decide whether the site converts. Discernment is the scarce asset now.

The bad version is generating the same shell for every client and calling it personalization. That is AI slop with better fonts.

Pick one marketing motion your team runs today. Something that runs serial, one step at a time. Ask yourself if AI could take it to parallel this month. Not next quarter.

posts.content:
I have a 2x2 I run on every prospect before I send a proposal. Most outbound teams are working three of the four quadrants. Only one of them actually closes a deal.

The axes are simple. Pain awareness on one side. Buying urgency on the other.

Quadrant 1. Window Shopping. Low on both. They are reading your content because they enjoy your content. They will never sign anything. Do not sell to them. Do not even pitch them. They're an audience.

Quadrant 2. Educated Bystander. They know the pain exists. They have read the books. They will take every meeting you put on the calendar. They will not buy. Nurture them; do not pitch them.

Quadrant 3. Panic Without Plan. High urgency, low awareness. They feel something is wrong but cannot name what. These are the ones who buy fast and churn at 90 days. They sign because of the panic. They leave because the panic did not match the cure. Disqualify or refer out.

Quadrant 4. The Painpoint Position. High awareness. Real urgency. They own the metric. They hold the budget. They can describe the pain in their own words, and they can describe what good looks like at twelve months. This is the only quadrant where you have a deal.

The rule I use now. If my prospect cannot describe both axes in their own words within ten minutes of a discovery call, I do not have a deal. I just have a meeting.

Before I sold B2B SaaS marketing, I sold houses.

In Houston. 2020 to 2022. A market that does not care if you went to the right school or used the right pitch deck. It cares about one thing. Did you find the buyer who could close, and did you find them before the other guy.

Then I sold credit card processing for 4 years. Door to door, phone to phone, restaurant owner to restaurant owner. A business where the average contract is small, the churn is brutal, and the only way to make a living is to understand the math of every account before you walk in, because CC processing is just a commodity.

Eleven years before I ever wrote the words ACV, MQL, or LTV in a Slack channel, I was running the same ROI equations under different names.

Average ticket. Acquisition cost. Payback period. Annual retention.

The vocabulary changed when I got to Kalungi. The math did not.

Here is what nobody at the B2B SaaS conferences tells you. The best ACV training academy in the world is selling something small to someone who is one bad month from cutting it. Because in that world, there is no demand gen team to bail you out. You either squeeze the unit economics out of every customer, or you don't eat that week.

Seven months into being Engagement Director at Kalungi, I am running the same math on demand gen engagements that I used to run on bank fee structures and 3 percent processor margins.

If you came up through the SaaS industry exclusively, your school of hard knocks was on a spreadsheet. 

If you came up through restaurants, real estate, or merchant services, you learned it standing in front of someone who could say no to your face.

Both paths get you to the same place. But one of them teaches you faster.

Part 1 of 4. Next Monday: the day I stopped chasing volume.

posts.content:
“You would become the CMO.”

I said that to a healthtech founder on a call last week. He was not hiring a CMO. He was weighing the cheaper-looking version of his marketing plan: a content shop here, an SEO agency there, paid ads with a third vendor.
Piece that together and the org chart quietly rewrites itself. Three vendors, each optimizing its own lane, none of them talking to each other. Somebody has to reconcile them into one strategy. That somebody is the founder, and he never applied for the job.

The cost stays hidden until the vendors start disagreeing. The SEO shop wants the homepage rewritten around keywords. The content agency just spent a quarter making it sound human. Guess who breaks the tie, at 11 pm, between his other nine jobs.

I watch this pattern across B2B SaaS companies at every size between $2M and $50M ARR. The vendors are usually good at their lanes. The gap is never execution. The gap is that strategy ownership was never assigned, so it defaulted to the person with the least available calendar in the company.

None of this is an argument against specialist agencies. It is an argument for sequence. Decide who owns marketing strategy before you buy marketing execution. Hire that owner, contract that owner, or accept in writing that it is you, and budget your week honestly for it.

Founders: how many marketing vendors are you running right now, and who reconciles them into one strategy?

author.name: Braison Murgai
author.info: AI & SaaS Revenue Engineer| Engagement Director @Kalungi

postedAt.postedAgoText: 1 month ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
Half the B2B SaaS founders I sat with this month are about to make the same marketing hire, and it is the wrong one.

They are hiring the strategic CMO first without the execution arm that should follow. Sharp brains, great deck, ten years of frameworks. And then, six months later, the pipeline hasn't moved. The founder starts wondering if it was the wrong person... It was not the wrong person.

It was the wrong sequence.

Two years ago, thinking was the scarce resource. Any B2B SaaS founder needed the strategic brain first, then handed the plan down to someone junior to build. That was the right order because generating a serious go-to-market plan took months and required somebody who had seen many.

Now thinking is abundant. Any founder can generate a defensible plan in an afternoon with the right template and the right prompts. What actually is scarce now is the person who will actually run the play. Send the third email. Ship the landing page on Wednesday, not next month. Follow up on the referral before it goes cold. Adjust the ad set on Monday after reading the report on Friday.

The premium moved from the deck writer to the play runner.

Which changes the hiring order inside a B2B SaaS company.

If you are at MVP and hiring your first marketing lead, hire the executor who can also think and has a CMO-quality brain. Grade them on what they shipped in the last ninety days at their last company, not on their frameworks or their title. If they cannot name three campaigns they personally sent live in Q1, they are the wrong first hire regardless of the pedigree.

If you are post-PMF and you already have two or three executors, that is when the strategic overlay pays for itself. The person who reads the board deck, sees what everyone else missed, and rewrites the plan. Sequence matters.

Hire the Quality strategist & Executor first.

This is not an argument against hiring top-tier strategist talent. It is an argument for pricing your team the way your own buyer prices you. Nobody grades your SaaS on the deck. 

They grade you on whether the product actually did the thing.

Where is your next marketing hire on the executor-to-strategist spectrum?

author.info: AI & SaaS Revenue Engineer| Engagement Director @Kalungi

posts.content:
Sitting in on a sales call. The prospect ends a 20-minute overview of their launch and asks a CMO on our team what the six-month plan should look like. The CMO opens their mouth. The prospect cuts them off.

'If you gave me the answer immediately upon hearing all of the inputs, that would be a disqualifier.'

It is the sharpest sales lesson I have heard this year, and it came from the buyer, not the seller

Here is the framework I am pulling out of it.

There are two speeds a serious buyer wants from you. The first is the speed of clarification. Ask the questions they did not think to answer. Push on the assumptions they buried in the pitch. Slow the room down while they are still watching.

The second is the speed of judgment. When they see you slow down to think, they trust the answer you give three days later. When they see you fire the answer back in real time, they discount everything you say for the rest of the deal.

Fast responses, fast recap emails, fast next steps. That worked when the buyer was a mid-market VP who wanted momentum. It fails at the operator level.

The operator buyer can already see the answer inside their own head. They are watching to see if you can see the same answer, and whether you can wait long enough to say it right.

The disqualifier was not a wrong answer. The disqualifier was a fast one.


Speed is a signal. Slow is a signal too. Choose which one you are sending.

What is the last question you asked a prospect that made them pause? I want to steal it 😂

posts.content:
First-month exercise we run on every engagement. Most agencies would've skipped.

Most campaigns therefore run on the outer ring forever. We call it Watering Hole Analysis. Three concentric circles. Each one a different layer of trust your ICP gives you.

The Outer Ring is Noise. Paid ads. Cold outbound. Display retargeting. Every other agency is fighting for space here. The cost per impression is going up. The trust per impression is going down. It is the easiest ring to buy your way into and the hardest ring to actually convert from. The

Middle Ring is Peripheral Vision. LinkedIn feed. Newsletters. Industry blogs. Your ICP sees you here. They might even click. They are not building trust here. They are scanning.

The Inner Ring is the Watering Hole. Peer Slack groups. Founder podcasts. Closed CEO chats. Private dinners. This is where your ICP actually trusts. This is where they decide whom to call when they need help next quarter.

The exercise. For your top-tier ICP, list the actual watering holes. Not the channels you are advertising on. The places your buyer would name if you asked them where they get unfiltered advice from people they trust. Two things almost always happen when teams do this exercise honestly. First. The list of real watering holes is short. Often five or six places. Sometimes three.

Second. The list does not match where the team's marketing budget is going. The work after that is not about adding more channels. It is about working inward. Earning your way from peripheral vision to the watering hole. That takes time, taste, and a real point of view. It does not take more budget. If you are a B2B SaaS marketing leader and your team is spending more than 60 percent of its budget on the outer ring, you do not have a demand gen problem. You have a trust geography problem.

What are the actual three watering holes for your top-tier ICP? Name them in the comments. Have a productive weekend.

article.title: Your Forecast Didn't Slip on Budget. It Slipped on Proof.
article.subtitle: Braison Murgai
article.linkLabel: Open article: Your Forecast Didn't Slip on Budget. It Slipped on Proof. by Braison Murgai • 5 min read
article.description: The four levels of proof, ranked by the trust they earnProof, when you are selling your software, is not a monolith. There are four levels. Your buyer

posts.content:
Wednesday night, I deleted three consecutive AI drafts of the same follow-up email.

They came out of the AI revenue sculpting system I use to run my pipeline, and I'd asked it for the one job I assumed it would be best at.

Every draft was written well.

Every draft explained the meeting back to the founder more carefully than the one before.

They were all solidly positioned drafts, but lacking the heartfelt connection to the other person who would be receiving my email

So I rewrote it myself, and it went out at 9:56 that night.

What I put in it: the report we built together, two case studies with hard numbers on them, four reference links, one person on my team he could meet with, and one clearly thought-through question only he can answer.

One sentence of my own made it in, and it was attached to a commitment I made to him rather than an arbitrary statement.

The subject line still reads "Following up on your playbook question," and the body draft never answered the playbook question... which was annoying

I'd already answered it on the call, and answering it again in writing would have asked him to sit through the same conversation twice.

That was humbling to notice in my own drafts.

Doing the explanation is the thing AI produces most fluently, and handing something to an AI to clearly represent what I truly wanted in the draft requires real context to produce a high-quality email to a potential client. 

If you're a founder and you've started letting AI write your follow-ups, you've probably read one back and felt it was somehow both correct and empty.

A follow-up is a clear, genuine, heartfelt touchpoint.

Every follow-up I send gets one scan before it leaves the inbox: every sentence that makes the touch feel void of the warmth that a real human has, and we keep what's left.

Try it on the next one you send.
